item.title: Flock Cameras Are Dividing U.S. Cities. Here’s What to Know About Them.
item.description:
Law enforcement agencies have embraced them. So have many cities across the United States, large and small.

But the proliferation of Flock cameras, a brand of automated license plate readers that employ artificial intelligence to identify and track vehicles, has divided the public and rattled civil liberties watchdogs.

Some say the cameras are a valuable tool to help catch criminals, while critics argue that they are an invasion of privacy, and that the information they collect can be misused by the government or rogue law enforcement officers.

Here’s what to know:

Flock Safety is a private company based in Atlanta that supplies many of the license plate-reading cameras used by law enforcement offices across the nation.

The company was valued at $8.4 billion as of April 2026, less than a decade after it was started by three graduates of the Georgia Institute of Technology.

More than 7,000 organizations in the United States have contracts with Flock Safety, according to the company.

The equipment, which relies on solar power or batteries and uses cellular networks, is normally leased, not owned. The camera systems can cost clients six to seven figures, including installation and subscription fees, depending on how many cameras are deployed.

Because Flock Safety’s cameras have so quickly spread across the country, “Flock cameras” has become a kind of shorthand for any cameras that use A.I. to identify and track license plates, though Flock is not the only company to provide the service.

And police departments are not the only customers. College campuses and homeowners associations have also put up the cameras.

Many of the cameras, known as A.L.P.R.s (for Automated License Plate Reader), use algorithms to read the letters and numbers on license plates, which are then cross-checked with so-called hot lists of vehicles that have been involved in crimes, including those reported stolen.

The cameras usually rely on infrared technology to help distinguish characters against the reflective backgrounds of license plates.

On its website, Flock says its cameras can detect vehicles up to 75 feet away. The devices are capable of capturing partial license plate numbers, vehicle makes, models, colors, alterations, times and locations, according to the company.

Flock cameras can be integrated with technology platforms from other companies, including automated speed enforcement systems that catch motorists who drive too fast.

Law enforcement investigators have credited A.L.P.R.s with providing critical leads in a number of high-profile cases, including the manhunt for Ryan Routh, who was sentenced to life in prison for plotting to assassinate Donald J. Trump at one of his Florida golf courses in 2024. The International Association of Chiefs of Police has endorsed the technology, describing it in the group’s magazine as a “crime-fighting star.”

The primary criticism of the cameras is similar to one of their key selling points: that they produce a trove of highly sophisticated surveillance records instantly. While proponents say this helps prevent crime, opponents say the information can be dangerous in the wrong hands.

That criticism has intensified as the Trump administration has carried out immigration crackdowns across the nation, fueling concerns about clients sharing license plate information with Immigration and Customs Enforcement and other federal agencies.

Flock has challenged that narrative, declaring on its website that it does not work with ICE. By default, the data collected from the cameras is not shared with federal agencies, according to the company, which said that communities or organizations using the technology get to decide what happens with the data. In some states, Flock’s technology warns users that its cameras cannot be searched for “immigration enforcement.”

Civil liberties watchdogs are unconvinced, contending that ICE can simply ask local police for the license plate data.

In Washington State, at least seven police departments and one sheriff’s office had granted access to the U.S. Border Patrol to their license plate reader networks in 2025, according to an analysis by the University of Washington. An audit by the city of Columbus, Ohio, found that its Flock data had been searched more than 15,000 times for potential immigration-related purposes since 2024.

Several law enforcement officers have been disciplined for misusing data from Flock’s cameras, including an officer in Milwaukee who was criminally charged after using camera data to track someone he was dating and the person’s ex.

Flock has sought to assuage the concerns of its customers by introducing so-called transparency portals that allow its clients to share audit data from the system with the public, said Torin Monahan, co-editor-in-chief of Surveillance and Society, an academic journal, and a professor in the department of communication at the University of North Carolina, Chapel Hill.

“So they implemented a number of changes, like having more controls over who has access to data, and also an audit assist log to help police departments flag or determine quicker if someone is abusing the system, for instance, by stalking their romantic partners when, obviously, they shouldn’t be using the system in those ways,” Professor Monahan said.

Dozens of communities have either deactivated the cameras or canceled their contracts with the companies supplying them because of complaints about mass surveillance and what critics have called a lack of guardrails over who can access the information.

That opposition has spawned groups like DeFlock, which seeks to raise awareness about the cameras and map their locations. Opponents argue that the use of license plate readers enables the authorities to track citizens without a warrant.

“It is a form of a dragnet,” said Daniel J. Solove, a law professor at George Washington University Law School and author of “On Privacy and Technology,” which was published in 2025. The technology is testing the Fourth Amendment, which prohibits unreasonable searches and seizures, in ways the constitutional framers could never have anticipated, he said.

In Los Angeles, the nation’s second-largest city, officials suspended the use of 138 pole-mounted security cameras operated by Flock in July in the face of public backlash over control of the information collected by the system. City officials want to adopt more limits to the data that the cameras collect.

In February, the Amazon-owned home security company Ring ended a brief partnership with Flock that would have allowed homeowners to share footage from their Ring cameras with local police during investigations.

In several cities, including Verona, Wis., and Dayton, Ohio, officials resorted to putting bags over Flock cameras after opting not to renew contracts with the company.

Some people have vandalized the cameras. In Houston, at least six of the cameras have been cut down, ABC 13 reported. And in Troy, N.Y., the authorities said they were investigating the destruction of three Flock cameras, according to local news media reports. The vandalism occurred after the city’s mayor had used an emergency order to continue funding the cameras, defying the City Council’s decision to hold off on the possible renewal of a contract with Flock.

item.title: Consumer Debt Data Shows ‘Overall’ Health Amid Persisting Divides
item.description:
The latest report on overall household debt and credit by the Federal Reserve shows that American households, taken as a whole, are in solid financial shape. But clear pockets of weakness persist, with stress in auto and student loans especially acute for some.

Despite volatility in oil prices and economic growth, finances for the majority of homeowners are in a healthy state, the report showed. Mortgages make up the largest segment of consumer loans, constituting about 70 percent of the $19 trillion in U.S. household debt. Mortgage debt balances ticked down in the second quarter of the year. And most mortgage holders continue to benefit from fixed monthly payments, many of which were often financed or refinanced at low rates a few years ago.

This effect, which stems from the ubiquity of 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, has been a clear ballast for personal finances and a continued source of strength for the economy — even as elevated prices in general erode the purchasing power of both homeowners and renters.

Separate data released Wednesday showed that, when adjusted for inflation, recent wage gains have been erased. From July 2025 to July 2026, real average hourly earnings for workers have decreased.

Many would-be home buyers remain locked out of the largely frozen housing market, as a result of higher home prices and elevated mortgage rates. Another hurdle is strict underwriting standards from lenders who remain wary of providing credit to consumers with lower credit scores.

“The overall picture — the overall — has been remarkably resilient, when you look at debt and spending levels, but I think a lot of it is reflective of that ‘K-shaped’ economy,” said Sophia Kearney-Lederman, a senior economist at FHN Financial, referring to those households on the bottom leg of the metaphorical K having a much harder time than asset holders at the top.

”Wage growth has not kept up with inflation and those people are struggling and student loan holders have had a lot of ups and downs,” she added.

The Saving on a Valuable Education plan, a federal student loan repayment program, was put in place by the Biden administration to make monthly payments more affordable. Among other provisions, it reduced undergrad loan payment loads to 5 percent of a borrower’s discretionary income from 10 percent. And borrowers with original balances of $12,000 or less could have their remaining debt wiped out after just 10 years of payments, instead of the standard 20 or 25 years.

The tax bill that President Trump signed into law last year, and lawsuits the White House supported, looked to scrap the SAVE program; and those provisions went into effect on July 1, effectively ending SAVE.

The latest data from the Fed showed that the previous rapid acceleration in student loan debt balances cooled somewhat in the second quarter. But proponents of student loan forgiveness at leading nonprofits — such as Natalia Abrams, president of the Student Debt Crisis Center — say that 1 in 5 borrowers is now in default, and that they now expect those numbers will rise.

Auto loan balances also increased $28 billion in the second quarter to $1.7 trillion, and delinquencies rose slightly for auto loans, too. This is partly a function of how cars have become much more expensive since the pandemic, and how interest on car loans have become much more elevated since then as well.

“We haven’t seen these things creep into the bigger picture yet,” said Ms. Kearney-Lederman of FHN financial. “But it’s definitely something we’re watching, particularly the longer inflation stays elevated while the labor market remains not awful but not great.”

item.title: The Golden Age of Mexican Food Is Here. And It’s Complicated.
item.description:
Along the old path of Route 66, America’s mother road, the drive-ins and lunch joints of Oklahoma City look a bit different from the picture postcards in nearby souvenir shops.

In the state that gave us Sonic Drive-In, the carhop craze of the 1950s and ’60s has long since withered as customers preferred to drive-through to satisfy their fast-food fix. But in recent years, the strip of Western Avenue has been revitalized by another kind of menu: Instead of burgers and shakes, you’ll find superspecific varieties of tacos, tortas de albañil, traditional Mexican stews and tostadas de pollo.

El Primo Loco, a grilled chicken drive-through (right next door to a Sonic, as it happens) offers a tostada Siberia, made famous by its namesake restaurant in Monterrey. Hang a right onto Southwest 29th Street and you’ll find a paleta and bionicos dessert shop, a panadería and a Mexico City-inspired torta spot that’s a tribute to the beloved TV character El Chavo.

Bookending the scene are the markets La Aguascalientes Mercado de Carnes and La Aguascalientes Super Market, which feature dishes rare outside Aguascalientes, one of Mexico’s smallest states.

In a former drive-through oil change shop, Crudoolandia sells ceviches and aguachiles alongside Clamato cups and beers for customers to mix into micheladas to drink, well, anywhere but there (per local liquor laws).

“We’ve always wanted to capture that Mazatlán, Sinaloa vibe,” said Nancy Soto-Hallman, who opened the spot with her husband in 2012. “Of course, we don’t have seafood as delicious as Mazatlán’s — it’s one of the cities with the best seafood in Mexico. But we wanted to copy that style — the banda Sinaloense-style, the festive atmosphere.”

A little piece of Mazatlán in O.K.C.? A generation ago, that notion may have sounded unlikely. In 1980, fewer than 10,000 people of Mexican descent lived in the metro area. Today, that number is about 180,000, nearly 12 percent of the population. And the variety of culinary offerings across the city reflects the size and regional backgrounds of that community. The Mexican food scene here is booming, and Oklahoma City is hardly an outlier.

In the past 50 years or so, the population of people of Mexican descent in the United States grew nearly fivefold, from about 8.5 million to more than 39 million. And according to a Pew Research Center analysis in 2024, one out of 10 restaurants in the United States serves Mexican dishes, and about 85 percent of all counties have at least one Mexican restaurant.

That means a vast array of regional Mexican food can be found across the country, from the Gulf Coast to the Pacific Northwest. There are pocket-size food scenes in New Haven, Conn.; Charlotte, N.C.; and the Armourdale neighborhood of Kansas City, Kan.

Eleven Mexican restaurants in the United States received Michelin stars this year, including Californios in San Francisco, the only Mexican restaurant anywhere in the world to get three stars.

In just the last 15 years, the American palate has expanded well beyond combo plates and game-night nachos. Mexican food in America today is a dynamic cuisine all its own, created by Mexicans and Mexican Americans apart from Mexico — and as American as any food.

But there is a jarring split-screen. Just as Mexican food is flourishing in the United States, so are nativist politics. Latin Americans, including Mexicans and Mexican Americans working in hospitality, have been swept up in aggressive deportation campaigns that have been a pillar of President Trump’s second term.

The paradox is not lost on Gustavo Arellano, a columnist for the Los Angeles Times and the author of “Taco USA: How Mexican Food Conquered America.”

“Basically Mexican food now is where Italian food was in the ’90s,” Mr. Arellano said. “You had chefs showing people that there was all of this regional variety.”

He pointed to birria tacos as an example. They are a staple in Zacatecas, where his parents are from, but he never saw them in restaurants, even in Southern California, until the mid-2010s. Not long after that, he came across a list of the best places to find them in Boston, not historically a hotbed of Mexican culture. “I could never have imagined a day where such a regional specialty would become not just ubiquitous, but a cliché,” Mr. Arellano said.

“From the moment Americans tasted Mexican food, they have never wanted to move on from it,” he said. At the same time, he added, “You have the continuation of Mexican immigration into this country, but also the spread of Mexican people to where they were not before. Where there are more Mexicans, you are going to see a backlash. History has taught us this.”

The story of Mexican food in the United States really began with the American annexations of the Mexican territory that became much of the U.S. Southwest. In his book, Mr. Arellano chronicled the rise, starting in the 1800s, of Mexican purveyors like the Chili Queens of San Antonio and tamale wagons in Los Angeles. In the decades that followed, Mexican American cuisine evolved to cater to the brief lunch breaks of blue-collar crowds.

Entrepreneurs of Mexican descent began to serve generous, one-plate, multicourse meals — wet burritos, stuffed sopaipillas and cheesy enchiladas. By the 1980s, Mexican food was widespread, the margarita emerged as one of America’s most beloved cocktails and American corporations like Frito-Lay and Pace Picante made tortilla chips and salsa ubiquitous.

In the 1980s and ’90s, Oaxacan immigrants went to California to work in great numbers. Most were Indigenous, and they formed a large population and culture of transnational people known as Oaxacacalifornia. Lugya’h, Casa Gish Bac and Comedor Tenchita are just a few examples of restaurants that carry on the legacy of Oaxacan immigrants who helped make moles, tlayudas and quesillo famous in the United States.

This sharing of Indigenous traditions and stories through food also set an example for other Mexican immigrants to showcase dishes from their own regions, be it plate-size tacos placeros in New York, chorreadas in Compton or birria estilo Aguascalientes in Oklahoma City.

Today, there are thousands of Mexican restaurants in Los Angeles, where the cost of living is among the highest in the nation. So, like many other Americans, Mexican immigrants and their descendants have looked elsewhere for work and more affordable housing.

That’s what brought Salvador Alamilla’s family to Idaho. Mr. Alamilla started cooking at a Tex-Mex restaurant in Boise called On the Border — “avocado fries, taquitos, every fried thing that you can think of” — working his way up from dishwasher to several cooking positions.

When he opened his own restaurant, Amano, in Caldwell, Idaho, Mr. Alamilla wanted to hew to the foods his family used to make in Michoacán, in southwest Mexico. That meant short ribs, and lamb shanks roasted for 12 or more hours in an underground oven like the one his grandfather used. The distinctive wood-smoke flavors of the region are married to a depth of spice, “the way we grew up eating.” He’s even slow roasting papayas and guavas for a smoky, fruity cocktail.

The move was a bit of a gamble. “Because we are not in the L.A. Arts District, we didn’t start off with that ready audience,” said Mr. Alamilla, the restaurant’s chef and co-owner. “But over the years, I brought the community along with us on our ride.”

Turning diners on to such regional specifics would have been difficult for Mexican chefs a generation ago, particularly in Idaho, he said.

“There was different pressures to try to assimilate, because the food that they were eating in the back was probably different than the food they were serving,” he said. “But for us, as their kids, because we grew up here, maybe we’ve been a little bit more privileged, we feel like we can be ourselves more, or at least we want to be ourselves.”

The tensions of the political moment weigh on Mr. Alamilla, whose parents brought him to the United States as a 5-year-old using another child’s papers. He did not become a documented permanent resident until high school. In a town the size of Caldwell, he said, it’s not hard to know your neighbor’s views. He sometimes looks out at the dining room and sees people who he knows support the ICE deportation campaign.

“It gives me a lot of sadness,” he said, “that the same people who want our people to be deported are the same people that are enjoying a chile colorado.”

At 7:30 on an overcast Sunday evening in March, the line was 40 deep at El Volcancito, one of the busiest tacos al pastor stands in East Charlotte, N.C. The stand is near the impressive Pulga Rodeo, a Mexican flea market teeming with regional cuisine, including Mexico City-style quesadillas at Los Machetes and soursop ice cream at Don Ruby.

Standing at the trompo, a standing spit of roasting pork, the taquero Daniel González said he honed his craft in Los Angeles’s competitive street-food scene at a chain of tacos al pastor vendors that are among the best in Southern California. “I was at La Güera out there in Los Angeles,” said Mr. González, smiling with pride as he turned the trompo to cook his mound of marinated pork.

As Mr. Gonzalez flicked small chunks of pineapple from atop the vertical spit and caught them on corn tortillas lined with strips of freshly carved pork, a woman in line exclaimed that they were just like the ones in Los Angeles, a sentiment echoed by many on TikTok.

Crowding around the salsa bar and huddling onto patches of grass to eat tacos standing up, locals debate whether Charlotte’s best al pastor is at El Volcancito, El Nazareno, Tacos El Regio, Compa Tacos or La Cumbre. But the fact that there is such a debate — in a county that had fewer than 7,000 Hispanic residents, according to the 1990 census — tells much of the story. Today, that population is around 60,000.

Maria Hernández, who owns El Volcancito, said she doesn’t mind the healthy competition. In the local al pastor scene, “el sol sale para todos,” she said — “the sun shines for everyone.”

The budding culinary renaissance has reconnected many Mexican American chefs with their home country’s cuisine. Gustavo Romero built his career cooking Italian after immigrating to the United States as a teenager from Hidalgo, Mexico. The first time he cooked Mexican food professionally was in 2017, at Calavera, a Oaxacan restaurant in Oakland, Calif.

“I understood more about myself through the process,” he said.

The experience led Mr. Romero to start Nixta Tortilleria with his wife, Kate, in Minneapolis, in 2020. Oro by Nixta, a full-service restaurant, followed three years later. Customers come from across the metro area to visit the side-by-side storefronts in northeast Minneapolis, both fueled by Mr. Romero’s passion for heirloom Mexican corn.

“We started treating the tortilla the way you treat a baguette,” Mr. Romero said.

Carlos Salgado helped create the surge of American chefs learning to nixtamalize heirloom Mexican corn to make tortillas in the traditional, labor-intensive way in his 10 years cooking at Taco Maria, in Orange County, Calif. The chef and his wife, Emilie Coulson Salgado, closed the Michelin-starred restaurant in 2023, and moved to Ms. Salgado’s native Door County, Wis.

La Sirena, their new restaurant, is finishing its second summer in Ephraim, population roughly 400. Wind blew in off nearby Eagle Harbor in late May, as diners filled the 22-seat restaurant for the evening’s featured dish: arrachera con mole negro, made with Wisconsin Wagyu and served with warm heirloom corn tortillas.

Door County, where the Hispanic and Latino population is around 4 percent, is a long way from Southern California. But Mr. Salgado said he’s as inspired as he ever has been to cook world-class Mexican food.

“It’s not an exaggeration to say that we wanted nothing less than to substantiate this example of brown excellence in a place that maybe hadn’t seen it before,” he said, “kind of like Taco Maria did 15 years ago.”

If rural Wisconsin and East Charlotte seem like unexpected places for remarkable Mexican food, until fairly recently New York City may have been just as surprising. But today, the well-worn line that “there is no good Mexican food in New York” says more about the speaker than the city.

“Before, you would see these large menus with enchiladas, burritos, tortas, tacos and all of that,” said Tania Apolinar, a co-owner of Carnitas Ramirez in the East Village. Now one perfect dish is plenty, whether it’s her own carnitas from Michoacán, flour tortillas from Sonora at Border Town or chalupas from Puebla Chalupas Poblanas El Tlecuile.

One of the more vibrant concentrations is at Sunset Park Plaza, a makeshift mercado that on weekends occupies a vacant parking lot in southwestern Brooklyn. Sonia Cortés started the Sunset Park Plaza in 2025, after another outdoor market in the neighborhood was dismantled by local officials. Ms. Cortes, an organizer, was selling pozole from a pushcart when police restrictions forced her to pivot.

In 2024, Ms. Cortes and other vendors rented the space, where they now operate under tented stalls, rain or shine. “Why not create a safe space where vendors could work, support their families and share their culture without having to worry about being moved from the streets?” Ms. Cortes said.

The market is now home to 10 vendors, each with a different specialty. One stand offers mammoth tacos placeros, spilling over with rice, beans and chiles rellenos. Another toasts Oaxacan tlayudas over an improvised grill in wire fish baskets. It’s a cross-section of Mexican cooking that exists nowhere else in the city, where everyone sips home-brew tepache, a pre-colonial pineapple beverage served from coolers with a heavy ladle.

“It’s like having a little piece of Mexico,” Ms. Cortes said.

Luke Fortney contributed reporting.

Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

item.title: Inside the $12.5 Billion Deal for the Lakers
item.description:
Andrew here. There’s hand-wringing in Silicon Valley about how Chinese open-weight A.I. models may upend the economics of frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI. But a counterview is attracting less attention: Beijing could clamp down on these models, which make their internal settings public, if regulators decide they’re too hard to control.

Remember that China was remarkably permissive around cryptocurrency — right until it pulled the plug on the sector. So while new open-weight models from Moonshot AI, Alibaba and others are enjoying tremendous momentum, Beijing could suddenly change its mind about them.

That could drastically reset the A.I. narrative in Washington and Silicon Valley all over again.

It’s a good time to sell equity in a major sports franchise.

The latest proof came on Wednesday, when Josh Kushner, the venture capitalist, and Bob Iger, the former C.E.O. of Disney, said that they planned to buy the Los Angeles Lakers for $12.5 billion.

That’s a record price for a U.S. sports franchise. The deal underscores that some deep-pocketed buyers think the benefits of owning a world-renowned team outweigh the steep expense, Michael de la Merced reports.

How the deal came together: Kushner and Iger had been working on buying an N.B.A. expansion team in Las Vegas for months. But the rising price for that franchise had the two considering an alternative, according to a person with knowledge of the discussions: buying an existing team.

On Friday, Kushner called the financier Mark Walter, who bought control of the Lakers last year at a $10 billion valuation. Over the weekend, the two sides — who didn’t use investment bankers — hashed out an agreement, reaching one by Sunday.

But word of the deal leaked on Wednesday, forcing the sides to acknowledge the transaction.

Under the terms of the deal, Kushner is putting up personal money, and Iger may as well. Thrive Eternal, an offshoot of Kushner’s Thrive Capital investment firm that Iger is involved in, is also expected to be involved, though N.B.A. rules would cap its stake at 20 percent.

Investors are betting big on the power of big-name franchises. Consider the recent activity in sports M.&A.:

An affiliate of Apollo Global Management agreed this week to invest $2.6 billion in the New York Yankees.

The majority owner of Liverpool F.C., the English soccer team, is in talks to sell a stake to an investor group that reportedly includes Jeff Bezos.

Thrive Eternal’s first deal, announced in May, was an investment in the San Francisco Giants.

Thrive Eternal’s website hints at the appeal of what it calls “iconic franchises.” They can withstand technological disruption — in other words, the teams’ games are can’t-miss live events for their global fan bases. Their franchises can command top dollar for media and merchandise rights and more.

Iger is also a lifelong basketball fan, and as Disney’s C.E.O. he understood the power of franchises.

Walter may also have been under financial pressure to sell, despite owning the Lakers for just a year. Federal prosecutors have been examining loans made by his insurance business to a Chicago firm over potential disclosure issues, Bloomberg reported last week, citing unnamed sources.

Walter’s firm, TWG Global, has approached investors about selling assets to pay down these loans, Bloomberg reported on Wednesday, again citing unnamed sources.

The Lakers deal, if it closes, would accelerate that effort, Bloomberg adds, considering the team’s valuation is poised to jump 25 percent in just over a year.

Luigi Mangione is said to be in plea-deal talks. Mangione, who is accused of fatally shooting the UnitedHealth Group C.E.O. Brian Thompson, is discussing a guilty plea to avoid a federal trial, Bloomberg reports, citing unnamed sources. (He has pleaded not guilty.) Mangione still faces charges in state court in Manhattan; prosecutors there will probably oppose any effort by him to dismiss their charges on double-jeopardy grounds.

Anthropic investors reportedly anticipate a $2 trillion I.P.O. Unnamed backers of the artificial intelligence giant told The Financial Times that they expect the company to double its valuation from the current level when it goes public, as soon as the fall. In the meantime, Anthropic is in talks to buy Decart, an A.I. start-up, for about $6 billion, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources.

A plan to sell early access to President Trump’s social media posts is challenged. Plaintiffs including The Intercept sued Trump and several White House officials, arguing that a move to give customers access to the president’s posts on Truth Social violated the First Amendment. Truth Social has so far signed up around 10 customers, who would pay up to $100,000 a month.

Stocks notched higher on Wednesday after a tame inflation report was seen to relieve some pressure on the Fed to raise interest rates. Prices rose 0.1 percent in July from a month earlier, and 3.4 percent from the previous year on a seasonally adjusted basis.

Lydia DePillis, who covers the American economy for The Times, talked with DealBook about the key takeaways.

What is the headline takeaway from the report?

Inflation is easing from its height following the U.S. and Israel’s attack on Iran in the spring, but it remains far too hot for comfort and is running well above where it stood at the beginning of President Trump’s second term.

Does the slight easing of prices actually relieve pressure on the Fed?

Maybe, but not much. Inflation has been well over the Fed’s target for more than five years. And although economists expect it to come down slowly for the rest of this year, several members of the rate-setting committee have expressed the view that rates are currently too low.

(A lot rides on the next Consumer Price Index reading, which will come right before their September meeting.)

How much are the Iran war and tariffs showing up in inflation data?

Last year, inflation might have fallen back to the Fed’s target if it weren’t for tariffs. Their impact has been waning as prices have reset at higher levels to accommodate the extra import taxes.

But then the Iran war essentially replaced the fading tariff impact on inflation — not just through the price of gasoline, but also through items that heavily depend on oil, such as airline fares.

What will you be watching for in the next report?

Grocery prices, which fell slightly in July. That’s a good sign, but the resurgence in energy prices may be felt more in August, and companies are also looking to recoup margins they lost when fuel prices jumped earlier in the year.

Also, the artificial intelligence build-out has been popping up in some strange places, like laptops and software, and pushing the index up overall.

The artificial intelligence race is a high-stakes competition for capital and computing power that hinges in part on a central question: Which company’s A.I. model is the best?

Vals AI is one of a group of start-ups seeking to answer that query, by measuring models’ performance against a set of benchmarks. Did the newest version of Anthropic’s Claude edge ahead of the last iteration of OpenAI’s ChatGPT? Or vice versa?

On Thursday, Vals is announcing a $40 million funding round at a $400 million valuation, Sri Muppidi is first to report.

Andreessen Horowitz led the round, with the existing investors 8VC, Bloomberg Beta and Pear VC participating. HRT Ventures and NextLadder Ventures also joined.

Vals built an automated system to grade A.I. models against a set of tasks and rubrics. These tests can judge models’ performance on a range of tasks, including those focused on coding, law and finance. Vals says that this system makes it difficult for A.I. labs to game the tests.

Vals also announced a set of tests on Wednesday to measure A.I. models’ performance on child safety and mental health metrics.

The start-up offers its test results of major models free to companies in the market for A.I. But it generates revenue by charging A.I. labs, including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google, to test their models.

Vals also sells its service to enterprise customers, such as the legal A.I. start-up Harvey, and government organizations including the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, which pay for proprietary evaluations of their products.

The start-up said its revenue had increased eightfold this year, although it declined to share dollar amounts.

There’s a need for trusted third-party groups, said Rayan Krishnan, the Vals C.E.O., who compared his company’s service to the product-testing nonprofit Consumer Reports and the credit ratings agency Moody’s. Without an independent appraisal, businesses may be reliant on self-reporting from A.I. companies themselves, Krishnan said.

“You can’t have the carmakers making the crash tests,” Jennifer Li, a general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, said.

The competition is fierce. There are at least half dozen other start-ups vying with Vals to become the dominant name in A.I. model evaluation. That group includes Arena, which already has $100 million in revenue and has raised $250 million from investors including Andreessen Horowitz.

When Randall Lane abruptly resigned last month after 15 years as the top editor of Forbes, he said that it was “time to live the spirit of the brand and try something new.”

He didn’t say what had prompted that decision. And neither did Forbes.

Now we know. Lane was fired after the company learned that he had accepted a payment of about $6 million from the founder of a company that does business with the magazine, Ben Mullins reports for The Times:

Lane, the magazine’s chief content officer, was paid by RJ Shook, whose company, Shook Research, has teamed up with Forbes since 2016 to publish rankings of wealth advisers. The payment was made after Mr. Shook sold a majority stake in Shook Research to PPC Enterprises, a private equity firm, last August, two of the people familiar with the transaction said.

It isn’t clear why Mr. Shook paid Mr. Lane. According to a person familiar with Mr. Lane’s thinking, he considered the payment a gift in recognition of the advice he had provided Mr. Shook over the years.

Lane violated company policy by not disclosing the gift, a decision he told The Times that he regretted.

“I should have disclosed the gift, and failing to was a serious error in judgment. I deeply regret that, and I lost the job and team I love because of it. None of this changes how I feel about Forbes and the amazing people there.”

item.title: How Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner’s Friendship Led Them to the Lakers
item.description:
It started socially, as business relationships between millionaires and billionaires tend to do. And, in the case of Bob Iger and Joshua Kushner, who are buying the Los Angeles Lakers, a supermodel played matchmaker.

In early 2018, Willow Bay, Mr. Iger’s wife and the dean of the University of Southern California’s journalism school, became friendly with Karlie Kloss, the fashion model and entrepreneur. They bonded over Estée Lauder: The cosmetics giant was preparing to make Ms. Kloss one of its newest faces, three decades after Ms. Bay had modeled for the brand.

Ms. Kloss soon asked Mr. Iger for a favor: Would he sit down with her boyfriend? She was dating Mr. Kushner, the founder of Thrive Capital, an investment firm, and the brother of Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law.

“I think she thought he would benefit from some of my wisdom,” Mr. Iger, 75, said with a chuckle in a phone interview on Wednesday.

The two men are 34 years apart in age. In 2005, when Mr. Iger became Disney’s chief executive for the first time, Mr. Kushner was still a Harvard undergraduate. By Mr. Iger’s telling, however, it was a bromance at first sight when they met for lunch at Marea, a high-end Italian restaurant in Manhattan.

“I took to him right away,” Mr. Iger said. “Humble, extremely smart, easy to connect with. I quickly learned that he has a lot of wisdom of his own.”

On Friday, Mr. Kushner called Mark Walter, who bought a majority stake in the Lakers last year at a $10 billion valuation, a record for the National Basketball Association. Mr. Kushner, 41, proposed buying a majority stake in the team with Mr. Iger. Their offer, first reported by ESPN on Wednesday, valued the Lakers at an eye-popping $12.5 billion.

“As lifelong N.B.A. fans, we are deeply honored for the opportunity to become stewards of the Los Angeles Lakers, one of the most iconic sports franchises in the world,” Mr. Kushner and Mr. Iger said in a statement.

The deal marks a striking evolution in the relationship between two generations of moguls. Over time, a mentorship has developed into a flourishing business relationship in which Mr. Iger, one of the best-known executives in corporate America, operates within an investment empire built by the younger and lower-profile Mr. Kushner. The Lakers are their biggest undertaking yet.

A spokeswoman for Mr. Kushner said he was unavailable for an interview. His public comments about Mr. Iger in the past were relatively minimal. Mr. Kushner wrote on social media in April that Mr. Iger “leads with boldness and conviction because he knows what he is building and why.”

Although the Lakers are one of the most storied franchises in professional sports, they are navigating a generational transition. The team has won only one championship in the past 16 years — hard times for an organization accustomed to contending for titles. LeBron James, the face of the Lakers for much of the past decade, departed last month for the Philadelphia 76ers.

Before their sale to Mr. Walter, the billionaire chief executive of Guggenheim Partners, the Lakers were owned for decades by Jerry Buss or his children. Mr. Buss turned the Lakers into a revered global brand. Celebrities like Jack Nicholson and Denzel Washington are die-hard fans. The waiting list for season tickets lasts years.

Mr. Iger’s relationship with the N.B.A. is unusually personal. Adam Silver, the league’s commissioner, has been a close friend for more than three decades. It was Mr. Silver who introduced Mr. Iger to his future wife, Ms. Bay, in the 1990s, when she was hosting the television show “NBA Inside Stuff.”

Mr. Kushner is also a longtime N.B.A. fan. He bought a minority stake in the Memphis Grizzlies in 2019. He subsequently sold it and bought into the Miami Heat. Mr. Kushner and Ms. Kloss, who were married in 2018, have been photographed at Knicks games in New York.

A formal business relationship between Mr. Iger and Mr. Kushner began to form about five years ago, as Mr. Iger prepared to leave Disney for the first time. He had stepped down as chief executive in 2020, ending a celebrated 15-year run, and would relinquish his remaining duties as executive chairman at the end of 2021. Mr. Kushner began recruiting him to join Thrive.

In September 2022, Thrive announced Mr. Iger as a venture partner and said he would mentor entrepreneurs and help identify investments. Mr. Iger brought extraordinary access to Hollywood and corporate America, and vast experience buying and integrating companies, including Marvel, Pixar, 21st Century Fox and Lucasfilm. For his part, Mr. Kushner helped Mr. Iger deepen relationships in Silicon Valley, introducing him, for instance, to Sam Altman, OpenAI’s chief executive.

Mr. Iger was at Thrive for only two months. In November 2022, the Disney board abruptly asked him to return as chief executive, replacing his handpicked successor, Bob Chapek, who was flailing. Mr. Iger agreed to return and stepped down from Thrive.

Still, his relationship with Mr. Kushner kept deepening. In 2023, Mr. Iger joined Henry Kravis, the founder of the private equity firm KKR, and a handful of other rarefied investors in buying a piece of Thrive itself. Last year, Mr. Iger and Ms. Bay attended Mr. Kushner’s 40th birthday party at Katz’s Delicatessen in New York.

When Mr. Iger stepped down as Disney’s chief executive for a second time in March, he again went straight to Thrive.

“I fortunately had the freedom to associate myself with just about anyone,” Mr. Iger said. “But I wanted to be extremely selective. I didn’t want to associate myself with anyone who would run contrary to my own values or put my reputation in jeopardy.” (Mr. Iger remains on the Disney board. The company has said he will leave when his contract expires at the end of the year.)

Mr. Iger rejoined Thrive as Mr. Kushner announced an expansion: Thrive Eternal, a vehicle for long-term investments in iconic brands and cultural assets that can’t be replicated by artificial intelligence. (Think Disney theme parks.) Its first investment was a stake in the San Francisco Giants baseball team. In recent months, Thrive Eternal explored a bid for a prospective N.B.A. expansion team in Las Vegas, pivoting instead to the Lakers.

Along with working on Thrive Eternal, Mr. Iger has spent time in recent months on his $45 million superyacht, the Aquarius, and working on a follow-up to his 2019 memoir. On Sunday, he will travel to Anaheim, Calif., to be honored as a Disney Legend, joining a pantheon of influential company figures; he will also have his name permanently added to a window on Disneyland’s Main Street, the company’s highest accolade.

But his purchase of the Lakers with Mr. Kushner is clear evidence that his post-Disney life won’t look much like retirement. Instead, he has found another outlet for the dealmaking and ambition that defined his tenure at Disney.

Perhaps part of the attraction is that Mr. Iger recognizes something familiar in Mr. Kushner.

“He’s a friend, but I also love the ambition,” Mr. Iger said. “It’s infectious.”

item.title: In a Chinese Leader’s Death, Mourning for a More Hopeful Time
item.description:
In 1998, Zhu Rongji, then China’s premier, told the staff of an investigative news program that he was a devoted viewer. He went so far as to say that the broadcast had given him ideas for reforms.

He then challenged the Communist Party’s doctrine that the media should emphasize what it called positive reporting. “Did ‘mainly positive reporting’ mean that 99 percent of reports had to be positive?” he asked rhetorically. “Wouldn’t 51 percent be enough?”

“Without such programs, how can the people’s voices be heard?” he asked.

Mr. Zhu was not calling for an independent press, which the party did not permit. The investigative show, after all, was aired by the state broadcaster. But he made clear that he regarded critical reporting not as a threat to the government, but as essential to effective government.

After Mr. Zhu’s death on Wednesday at 97, Chinese people circulated that story alongside many others portraying him as a straight talker, an independent thinker and, in the words of one commentator, “the finest premier in China’s march toward modernity.”

Mr. Zhu, who served as premier from 1998 to 2003 under former President Jiang Zemin, was the forceful technocrat behind some of China’s most consequential economic changes. He pushed the country deeper into the market economy and the global trading system, laying the foundations for two decades of extraordinary growth. Those changes also caused mass layoffs, strengthened the central government and left enduring social and economic problems.

The grief was about more than Mr. Zhu himself. It was also about what he had come to represent: an era when China was opening to the world, officials could publicly acknowledge the country’s problems and the future seemed more prosperous and hopeful. In remembering that era, many people were also passing judgment on present-day China, which has become more closed to the world, less tolerant of criticism and far less confident about what lies ahead.

On WeChat Moments, the semiprivate equivalent of a Facebook timeline, my feed filled with tributes from former journalists, entrepreneurs and professionals.

An investment banker posted a black-and-white photo of Mr. Zhu and remembered “an era when the country was on the rise,” a shared memory, he wrote, that seemed “extraordinarily precious today.” “We were lucky just to have lived through it,” a real estate developer replied.

Others posted photos of Mr. Zhu and his boss, Mr. Jiang, leaning toward each other, whispering and laughing heartily. Some comments said that Chinese leaders in that era still showed a human touch. The images evoked a political atmosphere that appeared more relaxed, collegial and human than the rigid one under Xi Jinping, the current president.

Many of the WeChat posts came from people I know or have interviewed. I’m withholding some of their names for fear of causing them trouble. One lawyer asked me to stop contacting him on WeChat and to use encrypted messaging apps such as Signal instead.

On China’s more public social-media platforms, searches for Mr. Zhu’s name on Weibo and Xiaohongshu, or RedNote, produced sparse results dominated by state media. On Wednesday afternoon, a search I conducted on RedNote returned only 25 results. Some ordinary users omitted his name, posting only a photograph or referring elliptically to “that era” or “him.”

Nearly three decades after Mr. Zhu called the media “the people’s voice” and “a mirror for the government,” the public discussion of his own death appeared to be carefully managed.

The authorities have seen how mourning for former leaders could turn into criticism of the current one. After Mr. Jiang died in 2022, people remembered the relative openness and optimism of his era, drawing thinly veiled comparisons with Mr. Xi. Weibo restricted comments and deleted a popular post thanking Mr. Jiang for allowing Chinese people to watch “Titanic.”

When former Premier Li Keqiang died unexpectedly the next year, videos of him promising that China would remain open to the world were deleted. Comments calling him “a good premier for the people” were censored.

By the time Mr. Zhu died, the censors appeared determined not to let nostalgia for another leader from the reform era become a public referendum on Mr. Xi’s China.

Lu Yiheng, a Chinese political commentator based in Toronto, saw a bitter irony in that nostalgia. Chinese people once dwelled on the failings of the reform era and imagined that a new generation of leaders would build something better. “But who could have imagined,” he wrote on X, “that today we would be grateful simply not to be heading toward another Cultural Revolution?”

That reversal in expectations animated many of the tributes. Amid pervasive job insecurity, slumping consumption and the party’s tightening grip on private enterprise, what some people seemed to miss most was not prosperity itself but the belief that hardship would eventually produce something better.

In a WeChat post, an executive recalled graduating from college in 1998, when jobs were scarce and the government was shedding workers. As he looked back, he wrote, that year may have marked the bottom for China’s economy. “Hardship is not frightening,” he wrote, “as long as there is hope.”

The nostalgia fogs over the brutality of Mr. Zhu’s reforms. Yasheng Huang, an economist at M.I.T., told me that more than 30 million state-sector workers had lost their jobs, many before China had established a meaningful social safety net. He argues that Mr. Zhu later used wrenching reforms to address problems aggravated by some of his earlier policies.

“His economic legacy was very complicated,” he said. “He used his right hand to solve problems created by his left.”

A Shenzhen resident surnamed Jin wrote on WeChat about how family members lost their jobs or were hounded by creditors during the Zhu years.

Yet popular culture of the period urged workers to accept their suffering as a necessary sacrifice. A hit song told them to “start over,” while a nationally televised comedy sketch declared, “If I don’t get laid off, who should?”

Mr. Zhu once said he hoped to be remembered as “a clean official” who had accomplished a few practical things. Mr. Jin saw another side to such ambition. “Throughout history,” he wrote, “some of those who make ordinary people suffer most are clean officials determined to get things done.”

item.title: Alfonso Fanjul Jr., Cuban American Sugar Baron, Dies at 89
item.description:
Alfonso Fanjul Jr., the patriarch of a family that lost one of Cuba’s largest sugar businesses in the revolution of 1959 and fled to the United States, where, thanks to pluck and government price supports, they built an even vaster empire, died on Aug. 3 in South Florida. He was 89.

The death was announced by Florida Crystals Corporation, part of the privately held family business that Mr. Fanjul presided over. The company provided no further details.

A billionaire who called himself a farmer and lived a luxurious life in Palm Beach, Fla., where he docked a 95-foot yacht, Mr. Fanjul, known as Alfy, was co-chairman and co-chief executive of the family businesses alongside his younger brother José, known as Pepe.

Their two other brothers and sister also have interests in the empire, which includes the world’s largest cane sugar refiner and the Domino and C&H brands.

Alfy and Pepe Fanjul became major donors to both political parties in the United States, a lesson in realpolitik that they learned after Cuban Communists confiscated 90,000 acres of the family’s property as well as its mansions and an art collection.

“One of the reasons we get involved in American politics is because of what happened to us in Cuba,” Alfy Fanjul told Vanity Fair in an article published in 2011.

He gave generously to Democrats and was a co-chairman of Bill Clinton’s 1992 presidential campaign in Florida. Pepe Fanjul has donated more than $2.5 million to the political campaigns of President Trump, a longtime friend whose protectionist tariffs have benefited the Fanjuls.

Mr. Clinton and former Speaker Nancy Pelosi attended Mr. Fanjul’s funeral in Palm Beach on Saturday.

During one of the few in-depth interviews he gave to the press, Mr. Fanjul was described by Marie Brenner of Vanity Fair as having “the old-world manners of a Spanish aristocrat, a cool detachment that indicates he is accustomed to being in control.”

For decades, the Fanjuls attracted critics of their labor, environmental and business practices. Environmentalists accused Florida Crystals of spoiling the Everglades with chemical runoff from their 180,000 acres of cane around Lake Okeechobee. (As evidence that it was a good environmental citizen, the company pointed to a renewable energy plant that it built, as well as to sustainable practices on its farms.)

Even sharper criticism came from free trade advocates, who said the Fanjuls profited from import quotas that ensured American sugar farmers got an inflated price, some three times higher than the rest of the world’s price. The difference was said to cost American consumers billions of dollars a year. The libertarian Cato Institute called Big Sugar in the United States a “candy-coated cartel.”

The Fanjuls, usually speaking through public relations specialists, responded that they had built their business over decades of hard work and determination — in the best tradition of the American dream.

Mr. Fanjul was born in Havana on June 27, 1937, to Alfonso Fanjul Sr. and Lillian (Gómez-Mena) Fanjul. His parents’ marriage united two wealthy Cuban sugar families, whose properties included 10 mills, mansions and the Manzana de Gómez, a full-block commercial building in central Havana that is now a luxury hotel.

Alfy, who was sent to Fordham University in New York for college, was back home on New Year’s Eve in 1959, watching the fireworks at the Havana Yacht Club, when the Cuban dictator Fulgencio Batista fled the country ahead of the advancing Communists.

Mr. Fanjul later told the story of a meeting in the family office soon after with Fidel Castro’s guerrillas, who opened the discussion by laying their machine guns on a table. The family lost all its assets and left for New York.

Mr. Fanjul, his father and his maternal grandfather, Pepe Gómez-Mena, set out to rebuild the business in America; they had already sent some money out of Cuba.

With other wealthy exiles, they raised $640,000 (about $7.3 million today) and bought 4,000 acres of land in western Palm Beach County and three run-down Louisiana sugar mills. The mills were shipped to Florida, where the first cane harvest was cut in 1961. Over the years, much of the cane was harvested by Jamaican workers on temporary visas.

Seven years older than his brother Pepe, Alfy became the leader of the Fanjuls’ rise in America. He took over as chairman and chief executive of the companies in 1980, after his father died.

The business expanded in 1984 when it acquired large holdings in Florida and the Dominican Republic from Gulf & Western, a conglomerate that then included Paramount Pictures. According to Forbes, in 2025 the family-controlled businesses were worth about $4 billion.

The family’s holdings also include a 7,000-acre luxury resort in the Dominican Republic, Casa de Campo, which is known for golf courses, a marina and an equestrian center.

The Fanjul portfolio includes a stake in Central Romana Corporation, a large sugar producer in the Dominican Republic. Last year, Trump officials lifted a ban that had been imposed by the Biden administration on imported sugar from Central Romana because of accusations that it used forced labor. Labor rights groups have said the company has not improved those practices.

Besides political donations, Mr. Fanjul gave to educational institutions and charities. He was a trustee of the University of Miami and the Brookings Institution, and a co-founder of Mission International Rescue Charities in the Dominican Republic. The Fanjul family has supported hospitals, schools and civic groups in Palm Beach County.

Mr. Fanjul’s marriage to Maria Cristina de los Reyes ended in divorce, and in 2007 he married Raysa Herrera, who survives him, along with his brother Pepe; their three siblings, Alexander, Andres and Lillian Fanjul; two daughters from his first marriage, Crista Ryan and Lillian Fernandez; a stepdaughter, Raissa Enis; five grandchildren; and seven great-grandchildren.

From his waterfront home in Palm Beach, Mr. Fanjul liked to set to sea on his yacht and for big-game saltwater fishing. He was twice a member of winning teams in the Sailfish Club of Florida’s Gold Cup tournament, in 1979 and 2007.

Unlike some members of the Cuban exile community, he did not obsess over how to reclaim his family’s lost holdings on the island they fled.

“My father spent the last years of his life trying to figure out how to get to Cuba,” he told Vanity Fair.

But Mr. Fanjul understood that the family’s future was American.

item.title: Flock Announces Privacy Updates to Its Car-Tracking Cameras
item.description:
Flock Safety, a company facing increasing scrutiny of its nationwide car-tracking technology, announced several updates on Thursday it said would improve privacy protections and prevent misuse.

The company’s network of 120,000 cameras, which can read license plates, are used by 7,000 law enforcement agencies across the country. Police departments say the systems help solve crimes. But reports of misuse by law enforcement, along with anxiety over the technology’s ability to surveil ordinary people, have led to protests and prompted some cities to end their contracts with the company.

“I realized we had a responsibility to do more,” said Garrett Langley, chief executive of Atlanta-based Flock.

Some cities, including Los Angeles and Dayton, Ohio, have stopped using Flock cameras in order to prevent immigration authorities from gaining access to their data. To provide more local control, the company said on Thursday, it will allow individual police departments to restrict what other law enforcement agencies can see — allowing access to data to find stolen vehicles, for example, but not for immigration violations, the company said. It also is shortening the default time for data retention to a week, down from 30 days, though departments could change those settings.

Reducing the time that data is retained is a positive development, said Chad Marlow, senior policy counsel from the American Civil Liberties Union. But he noted that it was easy for police departments to keep the data longer.

The heightened local control, too, is “good in theory,” Mr. Marlow said, but has never been proved to work. A similar program was rolled out last year to block impermissible searches, he said, but Flock customers quickly found a workaround.

“When you put all this together, what you see is Flock treating privacy issues as public relations issues,” he said. “Flock is giving this response because it knows its company is in serious, serious trouble.”

Mr. Langley said the updates had been in the works for months. Although Flock announced steps to assuage privacy concerns, critics still view legislative changes as the ultimate avenue to rein in surveillance tech like Flock’s.

“What we need are laws,” said Barry Friedman, law professor and faculty director of the Policing Project at New York University. “The government should never be collecting our information without a law that gives it authority.”
